title: What is the Bronze → Silver → Gold (Medallion) architecture — Bronze (raw/ingested data, append-only), Silver (cleaned/validated/deduplicated), Gold (business-level aggregates/features, ready for consumption) — and why does each layer being rebuildable from the one below it give you reliability?

s1_definition.profdef: The Medallion architecture is a layered data design, typically on Delta Lake, that organizes a pipeline into Bronze, Silver, and Gold tables. Bronze holds raw ingested data exactly as received, append-only, preserving history and provenance. Silver holds cleaned, validated, deduplicated, and conformed data with a proper schema. Gold holds business-level aggregates, features, and marts shaped for direct consumption by reports, dashboards, and models. Because each layer is deterministically derived from the one below it, any upper layer can be rebuilt by reprocessing, which gives strong reliability and reproducibility.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank's data as mail. Bronze is the mailroom where every letter is dropped in exactly as it arrived, nothing thrown away. Silver is the sorting office where letters are opened, duplicates removed, addresses corrected, and junk discarded. Gold is the manager's desk where clean letters are summarized into a daily report he can act on. If the manager's report is wrong, he does not panic — he just re-sorts from the mailroom, because the raw mail is always kept.
s1_definition.oneliner: Bronze keeps the raw truth, Silver makes it clean, Gold makes it useful, and every layer can be rebuilt from the one below.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Medallion architecture is a layered data design, typically on Delta Lake, that organizes a pipeline into Bronze, Silver, and Gold tables. Bronze holds raw ingested data exactly as received, append-only, preserving history and provenance. Silver holds cleaned, validated, deduplicated, and conformed data with a proper schema. Gold holds business-level aggregates, features, and marts shaped for direct consumption by reports, dashboards, and models. Because each layer is deterministically derived from the one below it, any upper layer can be rebuilt by reprocessing, which gives strong reliability and reproducibility.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank's data as mail. Bronze is the mailroom where every letter is dropped in exactly as it arrived, nothing thrown away. Silver is the sorting office where letters are opened, duplicates removed, addresses corrected, and junk discarded. Gold is the manager's desk where clean letters are summarized into a daily report he can act on. If the manager's report is wrong, he does not panic — he just re-sorts from the mailroom, because the raw mail is always kept.

**One line to remember:** Bronze keeps the raw truth, Silver makes it clean, Gold makes it useful, and every layer can be rebuilt from the one below.

sections.s2_technical:
Bronze is the landing zone. You ingest source data with as little transformation as possible, usually just adding metadata like ingestion timestamp and source file name. It is append-only so you never lose history, and it is your insurance policy: if any downstream logic has a bug, you still have the original bytes. In code this is often `raw_df.withColumn("_ingest_ts", F.current_timestamp()).write.format("delta").mode("append").save(bronze_path)`.

Silver applies the real engineering. You parse and cast types, enforce the schema, filter out corrupt records, deduplicate on business keys, and conform values (for example normalizing account IDs and currency codes). A typical dedup is `bronze.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(Window.partitionBy("txn_id").orderBy(F.col("_ingest_ts").desc()))).filter("rn = 1")`. Silver is where data quality lives, so downstream consumers can trust it.

Gold is consumption-shaped. You aggregate to business grain, join reference data, and compute features or KPIs such as daily balance per account, fraud scores, or regulatory totals. These tables are small, fast, and tailored to a specific use. For example `silver.groupBy("account_id", F.to_date("created_at").alias("day")).agg(F.sum("amount").alias("daily_total"))`.

The reliability argument is the heart of the pattern. Each layer is a pure, deterministic function of the layer below plus code. If Gold is wrong because of a logic bug, you fix the code and rerun Gold from Silver. If Silver is wrong, you rerun Silver from Bronze. You never have to re-fetch from fragile source systems because Bronze is your immutable replay buffer. This makes pipelines idempotent and reproducible, which is essential in banking where auditors ask you to reproduce a number from months ago.

A senior nuance is that the layers also separate concerns and permissions: raw PII can be restricted to Bronze, Silver can apply masking, and Gold exposes only aggregates. Combined with Delta time travel, you get both lineage and point-in-time reproducibility.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives a raw CSV feed of card transactions that sometimes contains duplicates (the vendor resends) and occasionally malformed rows. If we loaded this straight into reports, totals would be inflated by duplicates. This is exactly why we need a Bronze layer that keeps everything raw and a Silver layer that deduplicates and validates.

Problem 2 — The risk team wants a daily spend total per account to flag unusual activity. They do not want raw rows; they want a clean aggregate. This is exactly the Gold layer's job.

Problem 3 — Last quarter, a bug in the aggregation logic produced wrong fraud totals. Because Bronze and Silver were intact, the team simply fixed the code and rebuilt Gold. This demonstrates the rebuildable-from-below reliability property.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`MedallionDemo`) that ingests raw transactions into Bronze, cleans and deduplicates into Silver, aggregates daily totals into Gold, and then demonstrates rebuilding Gold after a logic fix — all for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001).

##### 4b. SQL / Delta DDL Script

```sql
-- Three Delta tables, one per medallion layer
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS bronze_transactions (
    txn_id STRING, account_id STRING, amount STRING, created_at STRING,
    _ingest_ts TIMESTAMP, _source_file STRING
) USING DELTA LOCATION '/data/warehouse/bronze/transactions';

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS silver_transactions (
    txn_id STRING, account_id STRING, amount DECIMAL(15,2), created_at TIMESTAMP
) USING DELTA LOCATION '/data/warehouse/silver/transactions';

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS gold_daily_spend (
    account_id STRING, day DATE, daily_total DECIMAL(18,2), txn_count BIGINT
) USING DELTA LOCATION '/data/warehouse/gold/daily_spend';
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```text
# spark-defaults.conf
spark.sql.extensions            io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension
spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog
spark.sql.shuffle.partitions    8
```
sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/medallion_demo.py
# End-to-end Bronze -> Silver -> Gold demo for the National Bank of India.
import logging
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from layers.bronze import ingest_bronze
from layers.silver import build_silver
from layers.gold import build_gold

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("MedallionDemo")

BRONZE = "/data/warehouse/bronze/transactions"
SILVER = "/data/warehouse/silver/transactions"
GOLD   = "/data/warehouse/gold/daily_spend"

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return (SparkSession.builder.appName("MedallionDemo")
            .config("spark.sql.extensions",
                    "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
            .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                    "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
            .getOrCreate())

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    # Raw feed: note the DUPLICATE TXN-2 and a malformed amount 'NA'
    raw = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("TXN-1", "SAV2001", "50000.00", "2026-10-30 09:00:00"),
        ("TXN-2", "CUR3001", "25000.00", "2026-10-30 09:05:00"),
        ("TXN-2", "CUR3001", "25000.00", "2026-10-30 09:05:00"),  # duplicate
        ("TXN-3", "SAV2001", "12000.00", "2026-10-30 10:00:00"),
        ("TXN-4", "SAV2001", "NA",       "2026-10-30 11:00:00"),  # malformed
    ], ["txn_id", "account_id", "amount", "created_at"])

    ingest_bronze(raw, BRONZE, source_file="cards_2026-10-30.csv")
    log.info("Bronze rows (raw, incl. dup + malformed): %d",
             spark.read.format("delta").load(BRONZE).count())

    build_silver(spark, BRONZE, SILVER)
    log.info("Silver rows (clean + deduped): %d",
             spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER).count())

    build_gold(spark, SILVER, GOLD)
    log.info("Gold daily spend:")
    spark.read.format("delta").load(GOLD).orderBy("account_id").show()

    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/layers/bronze.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

def ingest_bronze(raw: DataFrame, bronze_path: str, source_file: str) -> None:
    """Append raw data unchanged + lineage metadata. Append-only."""
    enriched = (raw
        .withColumn("_ingest_ts", F.current_timestamp())
        .withColumn("_source_file", F.lit(source_file)))
    enriched.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(bronze_path)
```

```python
# File: src/layers/silver.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

def build_silver(spark: SparkSession, bronze_path: str, silver_path: str) -> None:
    """Parse, validate, deduplicate. Full rebuild from Bronze."""
    bronze = spark.read.format("delta").load(bronze_path)
    typed = (bronze
        .withColumn("amount", F.col("amount").cast("decimal(15,2)"))
        .withColumn("created_at", F.to_timestamp("created_at")))
    valid = typed.filter(F.col("amount").isNotNull())      # drop malformed
    dedup_win = Window.partitionBy("txn_id").orderBy(F.col("_ingest_ts").desc())
    deduped = (valid.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(dedup_win))
                    .filter("rn = 1")
                    .select("txn_id", "account_id", "amount", "created_at"))
    deduped.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(silver_path)
```

```python
# File: src/layers/gold.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

def build_gold(spark: SparkSession, silver_path: str, gold_path: str) -> None:
    """Business aggregate: daily spend per account. Full rebuild from Silver."""
    silver = spark.read.format("delta").load(silver_path)
    gold = (silver
        .withColumn("day", F.to_date("created_at"))
        .groupBy("account_id", "day")
        .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("daily_total"),
             F.count("*").alias("txn_count")))
    gold.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(gold_path)
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five raw rows including one duplicate (TXN-2) and one malformed amount (TXN-4 = 'NA').

Step 1: `ingest_bronze` appends all five rows verbatim plus `_ingest_ts` and `_source_file`. Bronze now has five rows — nothing is discarded, because Bronze is the immutable record of what arrived.

Step 2: `build_silver` reads Bronze, casts `amount` to decimal (TXN-4's 'NA' becomes null), filters out the null, then deduplicates on `txn_id` keeping the latest by ingest time, collapsing the two TXN-2 rows into one. Silver ends with three clean rows: TXN-1, TXN-2, TXN-3.

Step 3: `build_gold` reads Silver, derives the `day`, groups by account and day, and sums the amounts. SAV2001 gets 62000 across two transactions; CUR3001 gets 25000 across one.

Step 4: Simulate a bug fix in Gold logic. Because Bronze and Silver are intact, rerunning only `build_gold` from Silver produces corrected Gold without touching raw data or re-ingesting from the source.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-30 06:31:01 INFO Bronze rows (raw, incl. dup + malformed): 5
2026-10-30 06:31:03 INFO Silver rows (clean + deduped): 3
2026-10-30 06:31:04 INFO Gold daily spend:
+----------+----------+-----------+---------+
|account_id|day       |daily_total|txn_count|
+----------+----------+-----------+---------+
|CUR3001   |2026-10-30|   25000.00|        1|
|SAV2001   |2026-10-30|   62000.00|        2|
+----------+----------+-----------+---------+
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Medallion architecture is a layered way of organizing a data pipeline, usually on Delta Lake, into Bronze, Silver, and Gold tables. Bronze is the raw landing zone, append-only, holding data exactly as it was received with just a little lineage metadata like ingestion time and source file. Silver is the cleaned and conformed layer, where I cast types, enforce schema, drop malformed records, and deduplicate on business keys so that downstream consumers can trust the data. Gold is the business layer, holding aggregates, features, and marts shaped for direct consumption by reports, dashboards, and models.

The key engineering property is that each layer is a deterministic function of the layer below it plus code. That is what gives reliability and reproducibility. If a Gold number is wrong because of a logic bug, I fix the code and rebuild Gold from Silver. If Silver is wrong, I rebuild it from Bronze. I never have to go back to fragile source systems, because Bronze is my immutable replay buffer. This makes the whole pipeline idempotent and makes backfills and corrections routine rather than risky.

At the National Bank of India this shaped how we handled card transaction feeds. The vendor sometimes resent files, creating duplicates, and occasionally sent malformed rows, so Bronze kept everything while Silver deduplicated on transaction id and filtered out the bad amounts. The risk team consumed a Gold table of daily spend per account. When a bug once produced wrong fraud totals, we did not scramble to re-fetch data — we fixed the aggregation logic and reran only the Gold step from an intact Silver table. The way I phrase it in interviews is that Bronze keeps the raw truth, Silver makes it clean, Gold makes it useful, and because every layer rebuilds from the one below, the pipeline is reproducible enough to satisfy a banking auditor.
